hook: Pick one thing you keep saying you'll do. Let's find why you haven't.
title: Will, Skill, Opportunity

game.prompt: Think of one specific thing you keep saying you'll do. Answer every line for that goal only.

questions.q: Pick one goal you keep postponing. For THAT goal: I genuinely want it, even when nobody is watching.
If this goal got hard or boring, I'd happily drop it.
I could do a rough first version of this today.
I'd need someone to show me where to even start.
I have the time, access and permission to begin.
Something outside me (money, rules, a gatekeeper) blocks the way.

W.name: Fired Up, Building Up
W.text: Today the want is strong, but skill and access score low. Don't wait for both: build the cheaper one first, usually a small skill.

S.name: Skilled, Looking for a Why
S.text: Today your answers show skill, but little want and no open door. Ask whether this goal is truly yours, or borrowed from someone else.

O.name: The Open Door
O.text: Today the door looks open, but want and know-how score low. Check whether anything behind that door sparks your curiosity.

SW.name: Ready, Door Closed (for now)
SW.text: Today you want it and can do it, but the door scores shut. That's structural, not a flaw in you. Find another door, or build one with others.

OW.name: The Eager Apprentice
OW.text: Want plus an open door today: a great place to learn anything. Your next move is practice, in small, honest reps with feedback.

OS.name: The Capable Bystander
OS.text: Everything scores high today except the fire. No productivity trick fixes a missing why. Look for the reason that would make this matter to you.

OSW.name: Full Agency
OSW.text: All three pillars score high today. The only thing left is to start. Put the first 10 minutes in your calendar.

results.name: The Starting Line
results.text: No pillar scored strong today, which is common, especially after a hard stretch. It's a starting point, not a verdict. Raise the easiest one this week (often a tiny skill rep) and play again in 7 days.

mid.name: The Half-Lit Path
mid.text: Today all three pillars sit in the middle: nothing blocks you, nothing pulls you. Pick the pillar that would be cheapest to raise by one notch this week, usually a 10-minute skill rep, and play again in 7 days.

insight: Action needs a want, an ability and an open door; researchers named this triad in 1982. Most stuck goals miss one, and pushing harder on the strong ones may not fix the weak one.
model: Stuck? Don't push everywhere. Find the missing pillar: Will, Skill or Opportunity.
try_today: Write your goal at the top of a page, then one line each for W, S and O. Circle the weakest and take one step on it.

source.work: Blumberg & Pringle, The missing opportunity in organizational research (Academy of Management Review, 1982); adapted as the original QUMNI WSO framework, drawing on Self-Determination Theory and self-efficacy research

try_team: Each person writes one stuck goal and scores Will, Skill and Opportunity 1-5. In pairs, the helper may only offer help on the lowest score.

hook: A gifted kid grows up with no instruments. What happens to the gift?
title: Talent needs a door

game.prompt: Picture a child with a gift for music and a hunger to play, born in a place with no instruments, no teachers and no time off work. Does her talent show up anyway?
choices: Yes, real talent always finds a way
Probably not, or only in pieces
game.reveal: Usually not, or only in pieces. If you said yes, that's the story we're all told: we hear about those who made it, not the many with grit and no door. Gifts are spread widely; open doors are not.

insight: Stories where grit beats everything hide the many who had grit and no door. Seeing the missing pillar is kinder, and more accurate, than blaming people for not trying.
model: Talent and drive are necessary, not sufficient. Someone has to open, or build, the door.
try_today: Think of one person whose skill you admire but who lacks a door. Send them one lead, intro or resource today.

source.work: Gray, Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard (1751); Giddens, The Constitution of Society (1984); QUMNI WSO Framework

try_team: Each person names one door someone once opened for them (a teacher, a lift, a loan, an intro). Then list doors your group could open for someone else.

from_source.quote: Full many a flower is born to blush unseen, / And waste its sweetness on the desert air.
from_source.cite: Thomas Gray, Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard (1751), stanza 14
from_source.next_read: Stanzas 12-15, from 'Perhaps in this neglected spot is laid' to 'Some mute inglorious Milton'

hook: You have one hour to help a stuck friend. Where do you spend it?
title: Push the missing pillar

steps.scenario: Ana loves baking and is great at it. She wants to sell cakes at the local summer fair, but she has no stall. You help by…

options.text: Sending her an advanced baking class
options.feedback: Kind, but her skill is already strong. More of what she has won't get her a stall.

options.text: Giving her a pep talk about following her dream
options.feedback: Her will is already on fire. Encouragement is nice, but it isn't what's missing.

options.text: Asking the fair organiser you know if she can share a table
options.feedback: Yes. Will and Skill are lit; Opportunity is missing. One door does more than ten pep talks.

steps.scenario: Leo has free time, a phone and a language app already set up. He keeps saying he 'should' learn Spanish but never opens it. You…

options.text: Ask what he'd actually do with Spanish, and why it matters to him
options.feedback: Yes. Skill can be learned and the door is open; the gap is Will. A real reason does more than a schedule.

options.text: Make him a strict study timetable
options.feedback: Structure helps once he wants it. Right now it would be a plan for something he doesn't care about yet.

options.text: Pay for the premium version of the app
options.feedback: He already has the door. A bigger door won't make him walk through it.

insight: A QUMNI rule of thumb, not a research finding: two pillars are often enough to take a first step, and help on the third pays off most. People tend to push the pillar that's already strong because it feels comfortable.
model: Push the one weak pillar, not all three. Small help in the right spot beats big help elsewhere.
try_today: Ask someone stuck: 'Is it wanting, knowing how, or access?' Then offer help only on the answer they give.

source.work: QUMNI 2/3 rule: an untested rule of thumb inspired by Blumberg & Pringle (Academy of Management Review, 1982), whose own model says all three pillars interact

try_team: Each person shares one stuck goal. The group may only ask: 'Is it wanting, knowing how, or access?' Then offer one help aimed at that answer.

hook: Two of three pillars often get you moving. Can you spot who's close?
title: Spot the 2 out of 3

game.prompt: Does this person have at least two pillars lit?

items.text: Mia wants to run a 5K, has never run, and there's a park next door.
items.why: Will + Opportunity. Skill can be built on the way: start with walk-run intervals.

items.text: Sam plays piano well and has one at home, but stopped enjoying it after his exams.
items.why: Skill + Opportunity, but Will is missing, the hardest to borrow. Rest, then find his own reason.

items.text: Jo dreams of acting, has never tried, and no theatre is nearby.
items.why: Only Will. Build one more pillar first, like an online class or a local reading group.

items.text: Raj can fix bikes, loves it, and a neighbour just asked for help.
items.why: All three. Full agency: he only needs to say yes.

items.text: Lee has a free gym pass but no interest and no idea how to train.
items.why: Only Opportunity. An open door alone doesn't move anyone.

insight: A QUMNI rule of thumb, not a research finding: with two pillars lit, a first step is often possible and the third can grow on the way. Will is the exception: without a reason that's yours, the others rarely carry you.
model: Two pillars often make motion possible; if the missing one is Will, start there.
try_today: List three goals. Count the lit pillars for each. Start the one with the most lit today.

source.work: QUMNI 2/3 rule: an untested rule of thumb inspired by Blumberg & Pringle (Academy of Management Review, 1982), whose own model says all three pillars interact

try_team: Write five goals from the group on slips of paper. Sort them together by how many pillars are lit, then plan the first step of one 'two-lit' goal.

hook: Stuck on a goal? Maybe the reason isn't yours yet.
title: The Capable Bystander

questions.q: When I picture finishing this goal, I feel…

options.label: Like I've finally pleased someone else
Like I did something that matters to me

questions.q: If nobody would ever know I quit, I would…
The reason for this goal mostly came from…
When I describe it to a friend, I say…

zones.label: Borrowed goal
zones.text: Today this goal sounds borrowed. That isn't a character flaw. Find your own reason inside it, or consider letting it go.

zones.label: Flickering fire
zones.text: Today your answers mix 'want' and 'should'. Link the goal to one person or value you truly care about and see if the want grows.

zones.label: Real fire
zones.text: Today your answers show real want. If you're still stuck, look at Skill or Opportunity instead of blaming motivation.

insight: With skill and access in place, the missing piece is often a reason that's yours. Goals that fit your values tend to last longer. If nothing has felt worth wanting for weeks, talk to someone.
model: No productivity hack fixes a missing why. Find your reason, or free yourself from the goal.
try_today: Write: 'This matters to me because…' If nothing comes, that's information, not failure. Can it be dropped, changed or tied to what you love?

source.work: Deci & Ryan, Self-Determination Theory (1985); Ryan & Deci, American Psychologist (2000); applied in the QUMNI WSO framework

try_team: Each person says one goal as 'I have to…', then tries 'I get to… because…'. Goals nobody can rephrase may need a new reason, or a rethink.

hook: Practised for hours. Why aren't you better? Order a real session.
title: Practice That Actually Works

game.prompt: Put a good practice session in order
items: Practice just beyond your comfort zone
game.explain: This is the core loop of deliberate practice: narrow focus, a stretch, feedback, then correction. Repeating what you can already do feels good but teaches little.

insight: Hours alone don't build skill; focused practice with feedback does more. The '10,000-hour rule' is a myth Ericsson himself rejected, and practice explains only part of skill differences.
model: Skill grows at the edge: one sub-skill, a stretch, feedback, adjust, repeat.
try_today: Choose one tiny part of a skill you want. Do 5 focused minutes on only that, then ask someone for one piece of feedback.

source.work: Ericsson & Pool, Peak (2016); Macnamara et al., Psychological Science (2014); applied in the QUMNI WSO framework

try_team: Everyone picks one tiny sub-skill (a chord, a serve, five new words). Practise 3 minutes, then swap and give each other one piece of feedback.

from_source.quote: …it is from playing the lyre that both good and bad lyre-players are produced.
from_source.cite: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, ch. 1 (trans. W. D. Ross)
from_source.next_read: Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, chapters 1-2: how skills and virtues are built by practice

hook: Reading your notes again feels like learning. Is it lying to you?
title: Pull it out, don't pour it in

steps.scenario: In a week you need to know new material: words in a language, a certification topic, or how a new system works. You've got one hour. Which plan sticks best?

options.text: Read the notes four times, slowly and carefully
options.feedback: It feels great because it gets familiar. But in tests a week later, rereading lost to self-quizzing by a lot.

options.text: Read once, then close the notes and write what you remember, three times
options.feedback: Yes. Pulling it out of memory is what makes it stick. It feels harder, and that's the point.

options.text: Highlight the key parts, then reread the highlights
options.feedback: Very popular, but big reviews found highlighting adds little on its own. Turn highlights into questions instead.

steps.scenario: Your friend tries self-quizzing and says: 'This feels awful, I keep forgetting. Rereading felt better.' You say…

options.text: 'Then go back to rereading, it's less stressful'
options.feedback: Kind, but the smooth feeling is the trap: easy now, forgotten later.

options.text: 'Struggling to remember is the workout. That's how it sticks.'
options.feedback: Yes. Effortful recall feels like failing while it's building memory. Gaps you find are gifts.

options.text: 'Maybe you're just not good at memorising'
options.feedback: Meant gently, but forgetting during practice is normal for everyone, not a sign of low talent.

insight: In a classic study, students who reread a text recalled about 40% a week later; those who tested themselves recalled about 61%. Yet the rereaders felt more sure they'd remember.
model: Easy-feeling study often isn't learning. Pull it out of your head; don't just pour it back in.
try_today: Pick something you're learning. Close the book and write or say all you remember for 3 minutes. Then check the gaps.
try_team: End a meeting, lesson or onboarding session with a 2-minute brain dump: everyone writes the 3 things they remember, no notes, then compares.

source.work: Roediger & Karpicke, Test-enhanced learning (Psychological Science, 2006); Dunlosky et al., Improving students' learning (Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 2013)

hook: You're trying harder and harder. What if the wall isn't you?
title: Ready, Door Closed

game.prompt: Where's the blocker: something you can grow, or something in the way?

items.text: The qualification you earned abroad isn't recognised where you live now.
items.why: A rule, not a flaw. Look for bridging courses or paths that don't need it.

items.text: You keep skipping guitar practice since you stopped caring about the songs.
items.why: That's Will, and it's allowed to change. Pick songs you love, or take a guilt-free break.

items.text: You can only study after 11pm because you look after family every evening.
items.why: Time is Opportunity. Shrink the task or swap for a better slot, not more willpower.

items.text: You don't know how to edit videos for the channel you want to start.
items.why: That's Skill, and it's learnable fast with free tutorials and feedback.

items.text: The club you want to join only takes people who know a member.
items.why: A gate. Build doors: show up at open events, ask for an intro.

insight: When will and skill are full, more effort on yourself can turn into self-blame. Some walls are rules, money, time or gatekeepers. That's not an excuse; it says change the setup.
model: If you want it and can do it but still can't, the fight is structural. Change the setup, not yourself.
try_today: Name one outside blocker on a goal. Write two other doors around it: another route, person, or place.

source.work: Giddens, The Constitution of Society (1984); Bourdieu, The Forms of Capital (1986); applied in the QUMNI WSO framework

try_team: List the walls your team, class or family keeps hitting. Mark each 'something we can build' or 'in the setup'. Pick one setup wall and name who could move it.

hook: Rich kids vs poorer kids: how much likelier to become inventors?
title: The lost Einsteins

game.question: In the US, kids from the richest 1% of families vs kids from the poorer half: how many times more likely are they to become inventors?
game.explain: About 10 times. Differences in maths scores at age 8 explained less than a third of that gap: even among kids with top maths scores, the richer ones were still far more likely to invent. Exposure mattered: kids who grew up around inventors were more likely to invent, often in the very same field.

insight: Talent is spread widely; doors are not. In this US data, growing up near people doing the work was one of the strongest doors. The study is observational, but the pattern is large.
model: Ability is often not the bottleneck; access is. Seeing someone up close do the work is a door.
try_today: Find one person who does something you'd love to do. Ask them one question: 'How did you get started?'
try_team: Invite someone with an unusual job or hobby to talk for 5 minutes to your class, team or family. Ask: 'Who first showed you this?'

source.work: Bell, Chetty, Jaravel, Petkova & Van Reenen, Who Becomes an Inventor in America? The Importance of Exposure to Innovation (Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2019)

hook: A friend says 'I'm just not a speaker.' What actually helps?
title: Belief built by doing

steps.scenario: Your friend dreads speaking up in class or at family dinners and says 'I'm just not that kind of person.' You…

options.text: Tell them they're amazing and will be fine
options.feedback: Warm, and encouragement does help a bit. But words fade fast when the moment comes.

options.text: Suggest they say one prepared sentence the next time the group meets
options.feedback: Yes. A small success they create themselves is the strongest source of 'I can'. Then make the next step a bit bigger.

options.text: Send them a video of a famous speaker
options.feedback: Watching others helps most when the model is similar to them. A star can feel out of reach.

options.text: Say some people just aren't speakers
options.feedback: Meant kindly, but it locks the belief in place. Belief in what you can do changes with experience.

insight: Bandura found that whether you even try depends on believing you can, not only on real skill. The strongest builder of that belief is a small success of your own.
model: Believed skill decides if you try. Build belief with small wins you earn, not with pep talks alone.
try_today: Pick something you think you're 'bad at'. Do the smallest possible version of it once today and notice that you did it.

source.work: Self-efficacy: Toward a unifying theory of behavioral change (1977)

try_team: Each person names one thing they're 'not a ___ person' about and commits to its tiniest version this week. Next time, everyone reports back.

from_source.quote: …we become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, brave by doing brave acts.
from_source.cite: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, ch. 1 (trans. W. D. Ross)

hook: Where does your 'I can do this' actually come from?
title: Your four sources of belief

questions.q: I can remember recent times I did something hard and it worked.
I often finish small things I start.
I know someone like me who has done what I want to do.
I've watched someone at my level learn this and get better.
People I trust tell me they think I can do it.
Someone has given me specific, honest feedback that I'm improving.
When I'm nervous, I read it as my body getting ready, not as a sign I'll fail.
Butterflies before a challenge usually help me more than they hurt.

advice.0: Your own wins scored lowest today? Set a goal so small you can't fail, finish it, and write it down. Stack a few this week.
advice.1: Role models scored lowest today? Find one person a step or two ahead of you, not a superstar, and learn how they started.
advice.2: Support scored lowest today? Tell one supportive person your goal and ask them to check in with you in a week.
advice.3: Reading your body scored lowest today? Before a hard task, notice the racing heart and tell yourself: 'This is my body getting ready, not a sign I'll fail.'

insight: Bandura named four sources of 'I can': your own wins, seeing people like you succeed, encouragement, and how you read your body. Own wins count most; the others fill gaps.
model: Belief in yourself is built from four sources. Find your weakest and feed it.
try_today: Write down three things you did well in the past month. Read the list right before your next hard task.

source.work: Bandura, Self-Efficacy: The Exercise of Control (1997); Jamieson et al., arousal reappraisal studies (2010)

try_team: Go round the group: each person names one recent small win they saw someone else in the room achieve. Everyone leaves with wins they didn't notice.
